title_original: Kwame Brathwaite and the Proud Afros of Harlem
excerpt_original: In 1960s Harlem, photographer and activist Kwame Brathwaite turned the slogan "Black is beautiful" into a rallying cry by sending Black women with proud Afros down the runway and in front of his lens: his first European retrospective now lands at the Maison Doisneau in Gentilly,…

blocks.caption: Radiah Frye, a model who adopted natural hairstyles, during a photo shoot at AJASS Studios, circa 1970  © Kwame Brathwaite / Courtesy of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive and Philip Martin Gallery, Los Angeles

blocks.text: In 1960s Harlem, photographer and activist Kwame Brathwaite turned the slogan “Black is beautiful” into a rallying cry by sending Black women with proud Afros down the runway and in front of his lens: his first European retrospective now lands at the Maison Doisneau in Gentilly, just outside Paris.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Kwame Brathwaite.

blocks.caption: Original members of AJASS, from left to right: Robert Gumbs, Frank Adu, Elombe Brath (seated), Kwame Brathwaite, Fred K. Ward, and Chris Hall. AJASS Studios, Harlem, circa 1964 © Kwame Brathwaite / Courtesy of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive and Philip Martin Gallery, Los Angeles

blocks.text: The son of Barbadian immigrants, Kwame Brathwaite (1938–2023) grew up in the South Bronx. In 1956, with his older brother, the graphic designer Elombe Brath, he founded the African Jazz-Art Society & Studios, a collective of artists. “I was lucky,” he recalled, “to be part of an emerging art scene.” He shot the nights at Club 845, where jazz rubbed shoulders with poetry and African dance.

blocks.caption: "Naturally '68" photo shoot at the Apollo Theater with Grandassa models and founding members of AJASS, circa 1968 © Kwame Brathwaite / Courtesy of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive and Philip Martin Gallery, Los Angeles

blocks.text: In the basement of the Purple Manor, a Harlem nightclub, the two brothers staged “Naturally ’62” in January 1962, a show of fashion and African hairstyles. Before a packed house, the Grandassa Models, a troupe of activist models, swept down the runway in fabrics from Accra and Nairobi. “No more straightening,” sum up Yasmine Chemali and François Cheval, the exhibition’s curators. “Skin color is celebrated.”

blocks.caption: Grandassa model Deedee Little in a car during the Garvey Day celebration parade, circa 1965 © Kwame Brathwaite / Courtesy of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive and Philip Martin Gallery, Los Angeles

blocks.text: Heir to the Pan-African thinker Marcus Garvey, the Black nationalist activist Carlos A. Cooks held that “the culture of a people is revealed in the homage it pays to those who have devoted themselves […] to the cause of freedom.” Around 1965, Kwame Brathwaite photographed Harlem’s Garvey Day parade. In one frame, the Grandassa model Deedee Little sits enthroned in a pink convertible, ringed by a swarm of children.

blocks.caption: Bob Marley at the Soundcheck Festival, October 4, 1975 © Kwame Brathwaite / Courtesy of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive and Philip Martin Gallery, Los Angeles

blocks.text: In his portraits, Kwame Brathwaite pioneered, in the curators’ words, “a free way of representing the Black body.” Around 1970, the model Radiah Frye posed for him bare-shouldered against a sky-blue backdrop. Gaze lifted, she wears her Afro like a diadem and embodies “a new pride: reclaiming one’s own body and image.”

blocks.caption: Marcia McBroom, actress and model, during a photo shoot for the Stylistics album cover, New York, circa 1976 © Kwame Brathwaite / Courtesy of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive and Philip Martin Gallery, Los Angeles

blocks.text: For the cover of an album by the soul stars the Stylistics, the actress Marcia McBroom posed for Kwame Brathwaite around 1976, arms flung wide, in yellow and pink feathers. From the sidewalks of Harlem to the top of the charts, the photographer turned “Black is beautiful” into a hit.

“Black is Beautiful,” curated by Yasmine Chemali and François Cheval, is on view at the Maison de la Photographie Robert Doisneau in Gentilly (France) through March 14, 2027. Wednesday to Friday, 1:30 to 6:30 p.m.; Saturday and Sunday, 1:30 to 7 p.m. Free admission.
